Christina Callender's Testimony for

Kingsbridge Armory Redevelopment Hello Council, My name is Christina Callender, and

I am from Kingsbridge and a soon-to-be graduate of the nearby Lehman College and

have

been

engaged with this project through NWBCC. I’ve dedicated my studies and professional life to understanding and alleviating the strains on working-class communities much like the one I’m from. I’m deeply invested in projects that not only enhance economic prosperity but also improve the lives of the people who live here now. I'm in strong support for this project, however we have the opportunity to ensure that the current project is one that keeps its benefits rooted in The Bronx and a different model of development is exemplified through key efforts. To achieve that, I urge the commitment to a community benefits agreement

and for the City and the Developer to commit to the following: Firstly, there must be an accessible design.The Armory must be welcoming and usable for all residents, including those with disabilities. That means ramps, lifts, wide pathways, and clear signage designed in partnership with the disability community. Secondly, the project must ensure truly affordable, family-sized housing that prioritizes Bronx residents in leasing. This project cannot rely on inflated AMI. so there must be some measures to counteract this to ensure that “affordability” reflects Bronx incomes, so families here can actually qualify. Units must include two- and three-bedrooms. Thirdly, the project must emphasize local hiring and contracting. This means that jobs at every stage must go to Bronx residents, and businesses first. Contracts should be awarded to Bronxbased businesses, MWBEs, and worker cooperatives. Additionally, space needs to be made available for existing Bronx vendors to mitigate displacement and ensure that wealth circulates within our borough. Fourthly, affordable community access to Armory uses should be prioritized. Create pricing and access policies that lower financial barriers for Bronx residents: e.g., resident discounts, sliding-scale memberships, free community hours, and no-cost space allotments for youth, seniors, and local nonprofits so the people who live here can actually benefit from what’s inside. Lastly, the city must ensure that the public infrastructure surrounding the armory matches the

Armory’s project’s scale. The armory will draw thousands of people and the city must meet the demand. This could be done with increased bus service on the BX9 and BX22, expanded 4, B, & D train service, and safety officers to guide traffic and pedestrians during large events. The surrounding area also needs stronger sanitation services; more frequent pickup, public trash cans, and recycling bins, so the Armory remains an asset, not a burden, to the neighborhood. This project has the potential to set a new standard for equitable development in New York City, but this will only happen if the project commits to a signed community benefits agreement

and holds Bronx residents at the center. Thank you Christina Callender Christina Callender

Testimony of David Levers Director of Government Relations & External Affairs Bronx Community College – City University of New York Before the New York City Council Subcommittee on Landmarks, Public Sitings and Dispositions On the Kingsbridge Armory Redevelopment September 30, 2025 Good morning, Chair Kamillah M. Hanks, members of the Subcommittee, and community stakeholders. My name is David Levers, and I serve as the Director of Government Relations and External Affairs at Bronx Community College, where I am a member of the President’s Cabinet. It is my privilege to testify today in strong support of the Kingsbridge Armory Community Benefits Agreement (CBA). At Bronx Community College, our mission is to advance equity, inclusion, and public higher education as pathways to opportunity. The redevelopment of the Kingsbridge Armory is a once-in-a-generation project, and we believe it must be anchored in a clear commitment to the people of the Bronx through a strong, enforceable CBA. Opportunities for Youth For our students, and for the young people of the Bronx, this project must create meaningful opportunities. We are encouraged that the CBA includes: • Youth internships connected to Armory tenants and vendors; • Job training, workforce development, certification programs, and apprenticeships that prepare Bronx residents for lasting careers; and • Partnerships with local colleges, including Bronx Community College, to design direct pipelines from education into the workforce. These commitments should be legally binding within the Community Benefits Agreement to ensure accountability. Bronx Community College is ready to partner with the Armory and its tenants to shape these programs and deliver real results for Bronx families. Investments in the Surrounding Neighborhood The reality is that the Bronx continues to live with the effects of decades of disinvestment. A project of this magnitude has the power to reverse that history, but only if the surrounding neighborhoods are also given the resources they need to succeed.

That means: • Supporting small businesses facing the risk of displacement; • Investing in public parks that are still waiting for long-overdue improvements; and • Rehabilitating housing that remains in urgent need of repair. The City must pair this redevelopment with robust, visible investments in the Bronx to ensure the Armory benefits not only those within its walls, but the community as a whole. In closing, Bronx Community College proudly supports this Community Benefits Agreement because it reflects our mission and values — and because we know that when the Bronx is given opportunity, it thrives. This redevelopment has the potential to be a landmark investment not just in a building, but in the people of the Bronx. Thank you, Chair Hanks, and thank you to the Subcommittee for your leadership. I look forward to continuing this partnership and to answering any questions you may have.

Kingsbridge Armory: Written Testimony - Tuesday, September 30th 2025 Good morning, City Council, My name is Alexandra Maruri, and I have been a proud Bronx resident for most of my life. As a child, I witnessed and experienced the devastating decade of the fires that tore through the South Bronx. In 1980, my family moved to Kingsbridge Heights, where I spent my teenage years and early adulthood. The Kingsbridge Armory holds profound meaning, not just for myself, but for countless residents across our borough. Since opening in 1917, it has stood as a symbol of strength and pride in The Bronx. It has served as more than a military facility, it has been a community gathering place, a cultural landmark, and a witness to generations of Bronx history. And yet, for all its history, one thing has remained the same; the need for opportunity, access to good jobs and sustained community investment. I experienced this firsthand growing up in The Bronx, and I still see it today in the lives of our youth. Regardless of how much time has passed, our young people are still confronted by the many of the challenges, barriers, and limitations that I once faced. That’s why I am deeply supportive of the vision plan to provide youth an opportunity in the Kingsbridge Armory project. This is more than a redevelopment; it’s a chance to rewrite the future of The Bronx. To invest in our young people. Honoring our past while building a new path forward, unlocking the endless potential of our young people. This is a new opportunity to break free from the weight of the past, the cycles of poverty, high unemployment, youth disconnection, and to begin building a new future in The Bronx. We must ensure our youth have access to the tools that can truly shape their future; opportunities for employment, a clear path to entrepreneurship, access to technology, positive mentorship, and the ability to see themselves as agents of change. This isn’t just about creating jobs, it’s about inspiring vision, growing leadership, and building equity from the ground up. The Kingsbridge Armory is the largest and most promising redevelopment project in The Bronx, and we must push to get it right. For this generation, and the next. Let’s invest in our youth. Let’s give them a voice, new skills, and let’s give them the resources and opportunities I wasn’t given. Thank you, Alexandra Maruri Angellyh Yambo Foundation

City Council Public Hearing: Kingsbridge Armory September 30, 2025 Good afternoon, my name is Brenda Irizarry and I live in the Norwood section of the Bronx. I am a member of the Northwest Bronx Community and Clergy Coalition. The Kingsbridge Armory Project will bring economic development to the Bronx, however, our residents and small businesses need more. A community benefits agreement that ensures local hiring, living wage jobs, free public access to athletic facilities, 30 hours per week for Bronx residents and allow street vendors to sell their goods within the Armory. In addition to community benefits, the city needs to do its share to improve, support and upgrade the area and nearby communities. I urge the city council to consider the following recommendations: *Create a Stabilization Fund for local small business that will provide legal services and other anti-displacement measures. *Create a local Harm Reduction Plan to support persons that are experiencing homelessness, addition and mental health issues. *Designate the Armory as a Resilience Hub for extreme weather events. *Increase subway service on the B, D and 4 trains as well as buses along Kingsbridge Rd. *Upgrades to the Aqueduct Walkway and improvements to other local parks. In closing, a community benefits agreement and commitments by the city are essential to the Armory Project. Therefore, I urge the city council not to compromise our communities but strengthen them. Thank you for your time and consideration.

Dear Members of the Council, I'm writing today as a proud Bronxite to elevate the importance of the Kingsbridge Armory to the upliftment of our community. I have a connection to the Bronx that is indelible, dating back to my father's youth, growing up he rode the "L Train" to and from work, to visiting family on Decatur Ave. and spending endless days with my aunt on Gun Hill Road. I've spent most of my adult years in the Bronx, in close proximity to the armory as a Lehman College alum and adjunct professor, and I've never strayed far from the neighborhood. We have the opportunity to create true economic opportunities for our residents if we, as residents, have the opportunity to shape those opportunities. First and foremost, the armory should be utilized to support Bronx residents in obtaining skills that allow them to earn a livable wage. With the proposed combination of "maker space" (manufacturing) and workforce development, Bronx residents can remain in their community while gaining valuable skills. This would alleviate the stress of traversing across the city for this unique type of workforce development. Additionally, the retail space/storefronts, allow our small Bronx businesses to remain in the Bronx, without paying exorbitant rent, and help to keep our dollars in our community. Bronx residents/businesses should be considered first for space inside the armory to promote their businesses and services. Our youth need constructive outlets, as we see the rise of graffiti again and the endless list of senseless youth-on-youth violence. We need to bring back the spaces that Boys and Girls Clubs offered, that PAL offers, and increase weekend activities for youth that will keep them off the street but also help them shift their mindset to a growth mindset as they build community and friendship, not enemies. The armory, and its future businesses, could provide space as a Summer Youth Employment Provider (SYEP), again keeping our children in our communities and building upon the youth-based activities we propose year-round. We also need a space to provide digital literacy, at varying levels to learners of all ages. We have to move our people from solely being users of tech to being producers of tech. We also need an oversight committee, an extension of the NWBCC, to actively govern current and future projects in the armory to ensure we are not left out of the conversation. For far too long, we've been minoritized in the Bronx: our health has been compromised for years, we've born the brunt of New York's "slum cleansing" pushing us into cramped spaces in the Bronx and recreating "slums" while midtown gleems, our homes are often neglected resulted in endless tragedies.
